Prepare union causes, union terms, and post-union problems as three separate stages; build a mini-timeline from 1798 to 1922.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “Why did formal union in 1801 fail to resolve Ireland’s political problems?”
Do not say the 1801 union made Ireland politically peaceful.
Do not confuse Catholic emancipation (1829) with Home Rule; they are different issues separated by decades.
Do not treat Irish nationalism as one single movement; constitutional, revolutionary and unionist traditions all existed simultaneously.
A major rebellion occurred in Ireland in 1798 amid revolutionary and sectarian tensions.
The Acts of Union joined Great Britain and Ireland in the United Kingdom from 1801.
Home Rule became a major late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century political issue.
Most of Ireland left the United Kingdom as the Irish Free State in 1922, while Northern Ireland remained within the UK.
Treat 1801 as the beginning of a new constitutional phase, not a solution — the Irish question persisted and evolved for over a century afterward.

Catholic emancipation, the Famine, and Home Rule each represent a distinct stage of the same underlying unresolved problem, and should be kept analytically separate even while connected chronologically.
